learn.hook: Look closely at a fern leaf: each little leaflet looks like a tiny copy of the whole leaf. Shapes like this are called fractals!
points: A fractal is a shape that repeats itself at smaller and smaller scales (self-similar). Ferns, cauliflower florets, lightning and coastlines are natural examples.
Sierpinski carpet: split a square into 9 equal squares and remove the middle one. Repeat with each of the 8 remaining squares. After step n there are 8ⁿ squares left.
Holes in the carpet: 1 after step 1, 1 + 8 = 9 after step 2, 1 + 8 + 64 = 73 after step 3.
Sierpinski gasket: join the midpoints of an equilateral triangle's sides to get 4 congruent triangles and remove the middle one. Repeat. After step n there are 3ⁿ triangles.
Remaining area: the carpet keeps 8/9 of its area at each step, so (8/9)ⁿ after n steps; the gasket keeps 3/4, so (3/4)ⁿ.

example.q: A Sierpinski carpet starts as an 81 cm² square. What area is left after 2 steps?
steps: Each step keeps 8/9 of the area

learn.reallife: Mobile phone antennas are sometimes shaped like fractals so they can pick up many signals in a small space.

games.title: Fractal facts
items: A fern leaf is a natural example of a fractal.
Each leaflet looks like a small copy of the whole.
Joining the midpoints of an equilateral triangle gives 4 congruent triangles.
They are all equilateral with half the side.
The Sierpinski carpet gains area at every step.
It loses 1/9 of its area at each step.
After step 3 the Sierpinski gasket has 27 triangles.

quiz.q: How many small squares remain after step 1 of the Sierpinski carpet?
quiz.explain: The square is split into 9 and the middle one is removed, leaving 8.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to remove the middle square

quiz.q: How many small squares remain after step 2 of the Sierpinski carpet?
quiz.explain: Each of the 8 squares becomes 8 smaller squares: 8 × 8 = 64.
quiz.mistake: Adds 8 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: How many holes does the Sierpinski carpet have after step 2?
quiz.explain: Step 1 makes 1 hole; step 2 makes one hole in each of the 8 squares: 1 + 8 = 9.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the new holes

quiz.q: A Sierpinski carpet starts with area 81 cm². What area remains after 2 steps?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts only one ninth, once

quiz.q: How many shaded triangles are there after step 1 of the Sierpinski gasket?
quiz.explain: Joining midpoints makes 4 triangles, and removing the middle one leaves 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to remove the middle triangle

quiz.q: How many shaded triangles are there after step 3 of the Sierpinski gasket?
quiz.explain: Each step triples the number of triangles: 3³ = 27.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4 instead of 3 for each step

quiz.q: What fraction of the Sierpinski gasket's original area remains after step 2?
quiz.explain: Each step keeps 3/4 of the area: (3/4)² = 9/16.
quiz.mistake: Keeps 3/4 only once

quiz.q: Which of these is a fractal found in nature?
quiz.explain: Each small part of a fern looks like a smaller copy of the whole leaf.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any natural object is a fractal

teach.ask: Gappu drew a triangle, joined the midpoints and shaded the corner triangles. What should he do next to make a fractal?
teach.praise: Repeat with every shaded triangle, again and again — 3, 9, 27 triangles! My Sierpinski gasket is growing.
teach.nudge: What do you do with each of the three shaded triangles?

topics.title: The Koch snowflake and fractals in art

learn.hook: Start with a triangle, add tiny triangles to every side again and again — the snowflake's border grows forever, yet it fits on your page!
points: Koch snowflake: start with an equilateral triangle. Split each side into 3 equal parts and build a small equilateral triangle on the middle part (removing its base). Repeat on every new side.
Each step turns every side into 4 sides, each 1/3 as long. So the number of sides goes 3, 12, 48, 192, ... = 3 × 4ⁿ.
Each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3. A triangle of side 9 cm (perimeter 27 cm) becomes 36 cm after step 1 and 48 cm after step 2.

Fractal ideas in art and buildings: the Kandariya Mahadev temple at Khajuraho has spires made of smaller and smaller copies of the main spire; Fulani blankets from West Africa repeat diamond patterns at smaller sizes; the artist M. C. Escher drew shrinking repeated shapes.

example.q: A Koch snowflake starts as a triangle with side 9 cm. Find the perimeter after step 2.

learn.reallife: Temple spires, rangoli borders and mehendi designs often repeat a motif at smaller and smaller sizes — fractal art!

games.title: Fractals in art
items: The Kandariya Mahadev temple is at Khajuraho.
It is in Madhya Pradesh.
Fulani blankets come from West Africa.
Their patterns repeat at smaller sizes.
Each Koch step makes the perimeter smaller.
Each step multiplies it by 4/3.
The number of sides of the Koch snowflake is multiplied by 4 at each step.
Every side becomes 4 sides.

quiz.q: How many sides does the Koch snowflake have after step 1?
quiz.explain: Each of the 3 sides becomes 4 sides: 3 × 4 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Adds a side instead of multiplying by 4

quiz.q: How many sides does the Koch snowflake have after step 2?
quiz.mistake: Doubles instead of multiplying by 4

quiz.q: A Koch snowflake starts with side 9 cm. What is its perimeter after step 1?
quiz.explain: 12 sides of 3 cm = 36 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the sides become one third as long

quiz.q: The same snowflake (start side 9 cm): what is its perimeter after step 2?
quiz.explain: 48 sides of 1 cm = 48 cm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the side count by the original side

quiz.q: By what number is the Koch snowflake's perimeter multiplied at each step?
quiz.explain: Each side becomes 4 pieces, each 1/3 as long: 4 × 1/3 = 4/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses only the 4 new pieces or only the 1/3

quiz.q: Where is the Kandariya Mahadev temple, famous for its fractal-like spires?
quiz.explain: The Kandariya Mahadev temple at Khajuraho has small spires repeating the shape of the main spire.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up famous temple towns

quiz.q: Fulani blankets with repeating diamond patterns come from which region?
quiz.explain: The Fulani people of West Africa weave blankets whose diamonds repeat at smaller sizes.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without knowing the craft's home

quiz.q: What makes a design 'fractal-like'?
options: It has exactly one line of symmetry
The same shape repeats at smaller and smaller sizes
quiz.explain: Self-similarity — copies of the shape inside itself at smaller scales — is the key idea.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any pretty pattern is a fractal

teach.ask: Gappu drew a triangle and added a bump to the middle of each side. What should he do to make a Koch snowflake?
teach.praise: Split every side into thirds, add a triangle on the middle part, and repeat on all the new sides. Snowflake!
teach.nudge: How do you split each side? Which part gets the new triangle?

learn.hook: Imagine slicing one corner off a cube with a knife. How many faces, edges and corners does it have now? Close your eyes and picture it!
points: Cutting off one corner of a cube removes 1 vertex but makes a new triangular face with 3 new vertices and 3 new edges. So F = 7, V = 10, E = 15 (and 7 + 10 − 15 = 2 still).
Cut off all 8 corners and the cube has 6 + 8 = 14 faces, 8 × 3 = 24 vertices and 12 + 24 = 36 edges.
A prism has two copies of a base joined by rectangles. With an n-sided base: faces n + 2, edges 3n, vertices 2n.
A pyramid has one base and triangles meeting at a top point. With an n-sided base: faces n + 1, edges 2n, vertices n + 1.
Prisms and pyramids are named by their base: triangular prism, pentagonal pyramid, hexagonal prism ...

example.q: Count the faces, edges and vertices of a hexagonal pyramid.

learn.reallife: Gem cutters slice corners off crystals to make new faces — they must picture the result before cutting!

quiz.q: A cube has one corner sliced off. How many faces does it have now?
quiz.explain: The cut makes one new triangular face: 6 + 1 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the new face made by the cut

quiz.q: A cube has one corner sliced off. How many vertices does it have now?
quiz.explain: One vertex is removed and 3 new ones appear: 8 − 1 + 3 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the old corner disappears

quiz.q: A cube has one corner sliced off. How many edges does it have now?
quiz.explain: The new triangle adds 3 edges: 12 + 3 = 15. Check Euler: 7 + 10 − 15 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Adds only one edge

quiz.q: How many edges does a prism with an octagon (8 sides) as its base have?
quiz.explain: A prism with an n-sided base has 3n edges: 3 × 8 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2n, the pyramid rule

quiz.q: How many faces does a pentagonal pyramid have?
quiz.explain: A pyramid with an n-sided base has n + 1 faces: 5 + 1 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the base

quiz.q: A pyramid has 10 edges. What is its base?
quiz.explain: A pyramid has 2n edges, so 2n = 10 and n = 5: a pentagon.
quiz.mistake: Uses the prism rule 3n

quiz.q: A prism has 9 faces. How many vertices does it have?
quiz.explain: Faces = n + 2 = 9, so n = 7. Vertices = 2n = 14.
quiz.mistake: Uses the face count as the vertex count

quiz.q: All 8 corners of a cube are sliced off. How many faces does the new solid have?
quiz.explain: Each cut adds one face: 6 + 8 = 14.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the new triangular faces

teach.ask: Gappu sliced one corner off a cheese cube. He says it still has 8 corners. Is he right?
teach.praise: The old corner vanished but three new ones appeared, so 8 − 1 + 3 = 10 corners. Cheesy maths!
teach.nudge: What happens to the corner you cut? How many new corners does the cut make?

learn.hook: Hold a glass at eye level: it looks like a rectangle. Look down into it from above: it is a circle! Same glass, different views.
points: A solid can look different from the front, the side and the top. The top view is also called the plan.
A cylinder standing up: rectangle from the front, circle from the top. A cone on its base: triangle from the front, circle from the top. A sphere looks like a circle from every side.
A cube looks like a square from the front, side and top.
For stacks of cubes, count layer by layer. The top view shows how many columns there are.
A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid. Cylinder: a rectangle and 2 circles. Cone: a curved sector and a circle. Square pyramid: a square and 4 triangles. Cube: 6 squares.

example.q: Arjun puts 3 cubes in a row on the floor and 1 cube on top of the middle one. Describe the front view and count the cubes.
steps: Bottom row: 3 squares side by side
Top: 1 square above the middle one
example.answer: Front view: 3 squares with 1 on top of the middle; 4 cubes

learn.reallife: Architects draw front, side and top views of buildings, and sweet-box makers cut flat nets that fold into boxes.

games.title: Top view: circle or not?
buckets: Top view is not a circle
items: Cylinder standing upright
Cone standing on its base
Sphere
Steel tumbler standing upright
Cube
Square pyramid
Brick lying flat
Triangular prism lying on a rectangular face

quiz.q: What does an upright cylinder look like from the top?
quiz.explain: Looking down, you see only the round top face, so the top view is a circle.
quiz.mistake: Gives the front view (rectangle) instead of the top view

quiz.q: What is the front view of a cone standing on its base?
quiz.explain: From the front, the cone narrows from a wide base to a point, so it looks like a triangle.
quiz.mistake: Gives the top view (circle) instead of the front view

quiz.q: Which solid looks like a circle from the front, the side and the top?
quiz.explain: A sphere is round in every direction, so every view is a circle.
quiz.mistake: Picks cylinder, whose front view is a rectangle

quiz.q: Arjun stacks cubes: 3 in a row on the floor and 1 on top of the middle one. How many cubes does he use?
quiz.explain: 3 cubes in the bottom row and 1 on top: 3 + 1 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the bottom layer

quiz.q: Which net folds into a cylinder?
options: A circle and a curved sector
quiz.explain: The rectangle rolls into the curved side, and the two circles become the top and bottom. A circle and a sector make a cone.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the cylinder's net with the cone's net

quiz.q: Which shapes make up the net of a square pyramid?
quiz.explain: The square is the base, and the 4 triangles fold up to meet at the top.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the pyramid with a prism or cube

quiz.q: A cube with edge 3 cm is unfolded into a net of 6 squares. What is the total area of the net?
quiz.explain: Each square is 3 × 3 = 9 cm². Six squares: 6 × 9 = 54 cm².
quiz.mistake: Finds the volume (27) or uses only 4 faces (36)

quiz.q: Joseph builds a 2 × 2 × 2 cube from small cubes. How many small cubes can he see from directly above?
quiz.explain: From the top you see only the top layer, which is 2 × 2 = 4 small cubes. The bottom 4 are hidden.
quiz.mistake: Counts all 8 cubes, including hidden ones

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Why does my cylinder-shaped water bottle look like a rectangle sometimes and a circle at other times?
teach.praise: From the front it looks like a rectangle, and from the top it looks like a circle. It depends on the view! Clever!
teach.nudge: Where are you looking from when it looks like a circle? And when it looks like a rectangle?

topics.title: Faces, edges, vertices and Euler's formula

learn.hook: Count the faces, corners and edges of any box, add the faces and corners, then subtract the edges. You will always get 2. Try it on a dice!
points: A solid's flat surfaces are faces, the lines where two faces meet are edges, and the corners are vertices.
A cube or cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A square pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
A polyhedron is a solid whose faces are all flat polygons. Cylinders, cones and spheres have curved surfaces, so they are not polyhedra.
Euler's formula for polyhedra: F + V − E = 2. For a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.
A prism has two identical ends joined by rectangles. A pyramid has one base with triangles meeting at the top.

example.q: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 15 edges. How many vertices does it have?

learn.reallife: Gift boxes, tents, the pyramid-shaped roof of a temple and a cricket ball show the difference between polyhedra and curved solids.

games.title: Polyhedron or not?
items: Cube
Cuboid
Square pyramid
Triangular prism
Sphere
Cylinder
Cone
A round laddoo

quiz.q: How many edges does a cube have?
quiz.explain: A cube has 4 edges on the top, 4 on the bottom and 4 upright ones: 12 edges.
quiz.mistake: Counts faces (6) or vertices (8) instead of edges

quiz.q: A polyhedron has 8 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have? (Use F + V − E = 2.)
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: How many vertices does a square pyramid have?
quiz.explain: It has 4 corners at the square base and 1 at the top: 5 vertices.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the top point (apex)

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a polyhedron?
quiz.explain: A cylinder has curved surfaces. A polyhedron must have only flat polygon faces.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any solid shape is a polyhedron

quiz.q: A triangular prism has 5 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explain: F + V − E = 2 gives 5 + 6 − E = 2, so E = 9. Count check: 3 + 3 edges on the triangles and 3 joining them.
quiz.mistake: Adds F and V without subtracting 2

quiz.q: Meena wraps a cuboid-shaped gift box, covering every face. How many faces does she cover?
quiz.explain: A cuboid has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left and right.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the side faces, or counts corners

quiz.q: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 15 edges. How many vertices does it have?
quiz.explain: 7 + V − 15 = 2, so V = 10. Each pentagon end has 5 corners: 5 + 5 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs in Euler's formula mixed up

quiz.q: Can a polyhedron have 10 faces, 10 vertices and 15 edges?
options: No, because F + V − E would be 5, not 2
No, because 15 is an odd number
quiz.explain: Every polyhedron obeys F + V − E = 2. Here 10 + 10 − 15 = 5, so no such polyhedron exists.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of edges must be even (a triangular prism has 9)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: What is Euler's formula, and how can I check it on a cube?
teach.praise: Faces plus vertices minus edges is 2. For a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. Euler was a genius, and so are you!
teach.nudge: Which three things do you count on a cube? What do you do with them?

learn.hook: An ant wants to crawl from one corner of a box to the opposite corner along its surface. The shortest route is easy to find — if you unfold the box!
points: A net is a flat shape that folds into a solid. A cube has exactly 11 different nets, each made of 6 squares. Six squares in a 2 × 3 block is NOT a cube net.
Other nets: cuboid — 6 rectangles; tetrahedron — 4 equilateral triangles; square pyramid — 1 square and 4 triangles; triangular prism — 2 triangles and 3 rectangles; octahedron — 8 triangles.
Shortest path on a surface: unfold the faces the path crosses into a flat net. The shortest path is then a straight line, found with the Baudhayana–Pythagoras theorem.
Example: a box with a 3 cm × 3 cm base and height 8 cm. Unfold two side faces: the ant crosses a 6 cm × 8 cm rectangle, so the path is √(6² + 8²) = 10 cm.

example.q: An ant crawls on the surface of a cube with edge 1 m from one corner to the opposite corner. How long is the shortest path?
steps: Unfold two faces into a 2 m × 1 m rectangle

learn.reallife: Packaging designers draw nets to cut cardboard boxes, and engineers unfold surfaces to lay the shortest cables.

games.title: Cube net or not?
items: A cross: 4 squares in a column with one on each side of the second
A 2-2-2 staircase of squares
4 in a row with one above the 1st and one below the 4th
Six squares in a 2 × 3 block
Five squares in a row with one on top
A 2 × 2 block of squares with two more attached

quiz.q: How many different nets does a cube have?
quiz.explain: There are exactly 11 different ways to arrange 6 squares so that they fold into a cube.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of nets with the number of faces

quiz.q: Which arrangement of 6 squares is NOT a net of a cube?
options: A cross of 4 in a column with one square on each side
4 in a row with one square above the first and one below the last
quiz.explain: In a 2 × 3 block, folding makes squares overlap and leaves faces open, so it cannot form a cube.
steps: Try folding: two squares end up on the same face
quiz.mistake: Thinks any 6 squares make a cube

quiz.q: What is the net of a tetrahedron made of?
quiz.explain: A tetrahedron has 4 triangular faces, so its net has 4 triangles.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with a square pyramid

quiz.q: How many triangles are in the net of an octahedron?
quiz.explain: 'Octa' means eight: an octahedron has 8 triangular faces.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with 6 (cube faces)

quiz.q: Which shapes make the net of a triangular prism?
quiz.explain: A triangular prism has 2 triangular ends and 3 rectangular sides.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the numbers of triangles and rectangles

quiz.q: A box has a 3 cm × 3 cm base and is 8 cm tall. An ant crawls over two side faces from a bottom corner to the opposite top corner. How long is its shortest path?
quiz.explain: Unfold the two faces into a 6 cm × 8 cm rectangle. The straight path is √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the edges instead of using the theorem

quiz.q: An ant crawls on a cube with edge 1 m from one corner to the opposite corner. What is the square of the shortest path length?
quiz.explain: Unfolding two faces gives a 2 × 1 rectangle, so path² = 2² + 1² = 5 (path ≈ 2.24 m).
quiz.mistake: Uses the diagonal through the inside of the cube (√3)

quiz.q: What is the total area of the net of a 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm cuboid?
quiz.explain: The net has two of each face: 2 × (20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm².
quiz.mistake: Counts each face only once

teach.ask: Gappu wants to walk across a box from one corner to the far corner on its surface. How can a net help him find the shortest way?
teach.praise: Unfold the box flat, draw a straight line, and use the theorem. Shortest walk found!
teach.nudge: What happens to the path when the box is unfolded? What is the shortest path on a flat sheet?

topics.title: Projections, shadows and building from views

learn.hook: At noon your shadow is tiny; in the evening it is longer than you. A shadow is a projection — and it obeys some neat rules.
points: Projecting a point onto a plane means dropping it straight onto the plane. Projecting an object projects all its points.

When light falls straight down (a perpendicular projection, like the overhead noon sun), the shadow is never longer than the object: a 10 cm pencil's shadow can be anything from 0 (pencil upright) to 10 cm (pencil flat). Slanting evening light can make longer shadows.
Sunlight casts shadows that are parallel projections, so parallel rods have parallel shadows.
Matching views: a cylinder has a circle top view and a rectangle front view; a square pyramid has a square (with diagonals) top view and a triangle front view.
Building from views: if the top view of a stack of cubes is a 2 × 2 square and the front and side views each show two columns 2 cubes high, there can be up to 8 cubes, but as few as 6.

example.q: A stack's top view is a 2 × 2 square; its front and side views each show two columns, 2 cubes tall. What is the fewest number of cubes?
steps: Each of the 4 places needs at least 1 cube (top view)
Each front column and each side column needs a tower of 2
Two towers of 2 on a diagonal do both jobs

learn.reallife: Architects draw front, side and top views so builders can make exactly the right shape.

games.title: Shadow rules
items: A shadow (projection) can be longer than the object under the overhead sun.
A parallel projection is never longer than the object.
Two parallel rods in sunlight cast parallel shadows.
Parallel lines project to parallel lines.
A pencil standing straight up under the overhead sun casts almost no shadow.
It projects to a point.
A flat square tile held parallel to the ground casts a square shadow under the overhead sun.
It is projected without change.

quiz.q: Under the overhead sun, how long can the shadow of a 10 cm pencil be?
quiz.explain: A projection is never longer than the object. Upright gives a point; lying flat gives 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a shadow can stretch longer than the object

quiz.q: A stick stands straight up under the overhead noon sun. What is its shadow?
options: A line as long as the stick
quiz.explain: Every point of the stick drops onto the same spot on the ground.
steps: Vertical stick, vertical rays → one point
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the sun is straight overhead

quiz.q: Two parallel bamboo poles stand in the sun. What can you say about their shadows?
options: The shadows meet at a point
The shadows are always equal to the poles
The shadows are at right angles
quiz.explain: Sunlight gives parallel projection, and parallel lines project to parallel lines.
quiz.mistake: Thinks shadows meet like lines from a lamp

quiz.q: A square tile is held parallel to the ground under the overhead sun. What shape is its shadow?
options: A square of the same size
quiz.explain: When the object is parallel to the ground, the overhead sun projects it without any change.
steps: Parallel to the ground → same shape and size
quiz.mistake: Thinks every shadow is distorted

quiz.q: A solid has a square top view and a triangle front view. Which solid is it?
quiz.explain: A square base seen from above and a triangle from the front fits a square pyramid.
quiz.mistake: Matches only one of the two views

quiz.q: A stack's top view is a 2 × 2 square and its front and side views each show two columns 2 cubes tall. What is the greatest number of cubes it can have?
quiz.explain: At most 2 cubes stand in each of the 4 places: 4 × 2 = 8.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the cubes seen in one view

quiz.q: For the same views (top 2 × 2, front and side each two columns 2 tall), what is the fewest number of cubes?
quiz.explain: Two towers of 2 placed on a diagonal make every front and side column 2 tall; the other 2 places need 1 cube each: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every place must be 2 tall

quiz.q: Which solid can have a circle as its top view AND a circle as its front view?
quiz.explain: A sphere looks like a circle from every direction.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a cylinder looks like a rectangle from the front

teach.ask: Gappu's shadow at noon is tiny but in the evening it's huge. Explain what a shadow is and why its length changes!
teach.praise: A shadow is a projection made by light. At noon the sun is overhead, so my shadow is short; in the evening the light comes at a slant!
teach.nudge: What makes a shadow? Where is the sun at noon compared with the evening?

learn.hook: Can you draw a 3D cube on flat paper so it really looks solid? Isometric dot paper makes it easy — and lets you draw impossible shapes too!
points: Isometric dot paper has dots in a triangular pattern; each dot has 6 equally spaced neighbours.
On it, vertical edges stay vertical and the other edges slope at 30° to the horizontal. Equal edges of a cube are drawn the same length.
An isometric drawing of a cube shows 3 faces, 7 vertices and 9 edges; one vertex is hidden at the back.
Arrangements of cubes (like tetris shapes) are drawn cube by cube, starting with the front-most cubes.
The impossible triangle looks solid, but each corner joins beams that are at different depths. Each corner makes sense alone; the whole object cannot exist in 3D.

example.q: How many small cube faces can you see in an isometric drawing of a 2 × 2 × 2 cube?
steps: Each big face shows 2 × 2 = 4 small faces

learn.reallife: Video games, engineering drawings and furniture assembly guides often use isometric views.

games.title: Isometric facts
items: On isometric paper, vertical edges are drawn vertical.
Only the other two directions slope.
An isometric drawing of a cube shows all 6 faces.
It shows 3 faces.
Each dot on isometric dot paper has 6 equally spaced neighbours.
The dots form a triangular grid.
The impossible triangle can be built from three straight wooden beams.
It only works as a drawing.

items.q: Faces of a cube you can see
Vertices of a cube you can see
Edges of a cube you can see
Small faces seen on a 2 × 2 × 2 cube
Small faces seen on a 3 × 3 × 3 cube

quiz.q: On isometric dot paper, how are the vertical edges of a box drawn?
quiz.explain: Vertical edges stay vertical; only the other two sets of edges slope at 30°.
quiz.mistake: Slopes every edge

quiz.q: On isometric paper, at what angle to the horizontal are the non-vertical edges drawn?
quiz.explain: The two sloping directions make 30° with the horizontal.
quiz.mistake: Uses 45°, as in some sketches

quiz.q: How many faces of a cube can you see in an isometric drawing?
quiz.explain: Only the top and two side faces face the viewer.
quiz.mistake: Counts all the faces of the cube

quiz.q: How many vertices of a cube can you see in an isometric drawing?
quiz.explain: All 8 corners exist, but one is hidden behind the cube.
quiz.mistake: Counts the hidden vertex

quiz.q: How many small cube faces can you see in an isometric drawing of a 2 × 2 × 2 cube?
quiz.explain: 3 big faces are visible, each made of 4 small faces: 3 × 4 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Counts the small cubes instead of the visible faces

quiz.q: Why is the impossible triangle impossible?
options: Its corners join beams at different depths, so the whole shape cannot exist in 3D
quiz.explain: Each corner looks fine, but following the beams around shows they cannot all meet in real space.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the drawing breaks a rule of triangles

quiz.q: What pattern do the dots on isometric dot paper make?
options: A triangular pattern, each dot with 6 equal neighbours
quiz.explain: Isometric dots sit at the corners of equilateral triangles.
quiz.mistake: Confuses isometric paper with square dot paper

quiz.q: In an isometric drawing of a cube with edge 3 cm, how long are the drawn edges?
options: Only the vertical edges are drawn
quiz.explain: Isometric drawing keeps equal edges equal, so every edge of the cube is drawn the same length.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sloping edges must be drawn shorter

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw a tetris-shaped stack of 4 cubes so it looks 3D. How can isometric paper help?
teach.praise: Vertical lines straight up, the rest at 30°, and draw the front cubes first. My tetris block looks real!
teach.nudge: Which edges stay vertical on isometric paper? Which cubes should you draw first?

learn.hook: With just a pencil, a ruler and a compass you can draw a perfect 60°, 30°, 90° or 45° angle, without ever looking at a protractor!
points: A compass keeps a fixed distance, so every point on an arc is the same distance from the compass point.
Perpendicular bisector of AB: draw arcs of the same radius (more than half of AB) from A and from B. Join the two points where they cross. Every point on this line is equally far from A and B.
Angle bisector: draw an arc from the vertex cutting both arms. From those two points draw equal arcs that cross. Join the crossing point to the vertex.
60°: draw an arc from the vertex, then an arc of the same radius from where it cuts the arm. This makes an equilateral triangle. Bisect 60° to get 30°; bisect 90° to get 45°.
A triangle can be drawn from three sides only if any two sides together are longer than the third.

example.q: How can you construct an angle of 45° with a ruler and compass?
steps: Draw a line and mark a point O on it
Construct a perpendicular at O to get 90°

learn.reallife: Architects, carpenters and rangoli artists use compass constructions to get exact angles and symmetric designs.

games.title: Compass check
items: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and from B.
That is exactly what makes it the perpendicular bisector.
For a perpendicular bisector, the arcs must have a radius less than half of AB.
With less than half, the arcs from A and B would not meet. The radius must be more than half.
Bisecting a 60° angle gives 30°.
A triangle can be drawn with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm.
3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 8, so the sides cannot meet.
Bisecting 90° and then bisecting one half again gives 22.5°.
An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal parts.
Bisect means cut into two equal halves.

quiz.q: What angle do you get when you bisect a 90° angle?
quiz.explain: Bisecting cuts an angle into two equal halves: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle instead of halving it

quiz.q: Riya draws arcs of the same radius from points A and B and joins the two points where the arcs cross. What has she drawn?
quiz.explain: The two crossing points are each equally far from A and B. The line through them cuts AB in half at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the perpendicular bisector with the angle bisector

quiz.q: Point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and PA = 7 cm. What is PB?
quiz.explain: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equally far from A and B, so PB = PA = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Doubles or halves PA, thinking P must be the midpoint

quiz.q: Which set of side lengths can make a triangle?
quiz.explain: 5 + 6 = 11 is more than 10, so the sides can meet. In the others, the two shorter sides add up to the longest side or less.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any three lengths can make a triangle

quiz.q: To construct 60°, you draw an arc from the vertex and then an arc of the same radius from where it cuts the arm. Why does this give 60°?
options: It makes an equilateral triangle, and each angle of that triangle is 60°
quiz.explain: The vertex, the first cut point and the crossing point are all one radius apart, forming an equilateral triangle. Each of its angles is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Follows the steps without seeing the equilateral triangle behind them

quiz.q: Kabir bisects an angle of 130°. What is the size of each part?
quiz.explain: Bisecting means halving: 130° ÷ 2 = 65°.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle

quiz.q: Which construction gives an angle of 120°?
options: Make two 60° angles side by side
quiz.explain: 60° + 60° = 120°. Bisecting 60° gives 30°, bisecting 90° gives 45°, and a perpendicular gives 90°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bisecting makes an angle bigger

quiz.q: Aisha bisects a 60° angle, then bisects one of the halves. What angle does she get?
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first bisection

teach.ask: Gappu asks: I have lost my protractor! How can I still draw a 30° angle?
teach.praise: Make 60° with compass arcs (an equilateral triangle), then bisect it to get 30°. No protractor needed!
teach.nudge: Which angle can you make easily with just a compass? How do you get half of it?
